Neither Nvidia nor d-Matrix has confirmed it, and they haven’t disclosed the size or timing. The reported stake would follow similar arrangements with Marvell, Intel and Amazon. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [AI & Machine Learning](https://shattered.io/ai-machine-learning/) # TypeSafe AI’s Jev Hits $7.5B Valuation in Weeks [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/emarchetti.webp) [Dr. Elena Marchetti](https://shattered.io/author/emarchetti/) Updated Oct 10, 2026 · 13 min read A startup most people had never heard of a month ago just got valued higher than most publicly traded software companies. TypeSafe AI, the maker of a non-text AI model called Jev, has raised $870 million in a new funding round that values the company at $7.5 billion, according to reporting from TechCrunch, Reuters, and Bloomberg (via Investing.com). The round, led by Andreessen Horowitz with participation from Sequoia and existing backer DCVC, lands just weeks after Jev’s public debut, and it’s forcing a fresh conversation about what “AI model” even means in 2026. The headline number is eye-catching on its own. What makes it stranger is the product behind it. Jev isn’t a chatbot, doesn’t write essays, and won’t draft your emails. It doesn’t output text at all. Instead, built on a transformer architecture, it produces probabilities, what TypeSafe AI calls “calibrated decisions.” That’s a deliberate departure from the [large language model](https://shattered.io/category/ai-machine-learning/) playbook that has dominated AI headlines since ChatGPT’s debut, and investors are betting real money that the departure is the point. ## What TypeSafe AI and Jev Actually Are TypeSafe AI was founded in 2024 by three people with resumes that read like a checklist of the industry’s biggest labs. Diogo Almeida previously worked as a researcher at OpenAI. Sasha Sheng came from a research engineering role at Meta. Erik Gafni rounds out the founding team as an engineer and entrepreneur, according to the company’s own announcement. Two years later, the trio shipped Jev, and the launch video reportedly went viral fast enough to pull in a wave of interest from chief executives, developers, and investors almost overnight. Almeida described that moment plainly. “The launch video going viral led to a surge of interest from chief executives, developers, and investors,” he said, a comment that captures how quickly a niche technical demo turned into a boardroom conversation. The distinction that TypeSafe AI keeps pressing is that Jev is explicitly not a large language model. It doesn’t generate the next token in a sentence. It evaluates inputs and returns a probability-weighted decision, the kind of output a fraud-detection system, a logistics router, or a pricing engine might need far more than a paragraph of prose. That framing matters because it positions Jev against a different competitive set than [GPT-6](https://shattered.io/gpt-6-intelligent-ui-chatgpt-rollout-2026/) or [Claude Opus 5.5](https://shattered.io/claude-opus-5-5-beats-gpt-5-6-sol-benchmark-2026/). Those systems compete on reasoning depth, context windows, and conversational nuance. Jev, as described by TypeSafe AI, competes on speed and cost for narrow, structured decisions, the unglamorous but high-volume work that sits behind a lot of enterprise software. ## The $870 Million Round, Broken Down The size of the round alone puts TypeSafe AI in rarefied company for a startup barely two years old. Andreessen Horowitz led the investment, with Sequoia joining as a new backer alongside DCVC, which had already invested in an earlier round, per the company’s statement. None of the three firms are strangers to swinging big on AI infrastructure bets, but a16z’s decision to lead here is notable given how selective the firm has been about which foundation-model companies it backs directly versus through its broader portfolio. highlights.content: # AI agents can be unpredictable. Your control layer shouldn't be. In multi-agent systems, agents can be individually correct and still produce a wrong result when they work together. One agent’s output becomes another agent’s context. Information can be lost or misinterpreted during a handoff, shared state can drift, and agents can get stuck in loops or deadlocks. When several agents rely on the same underlying model, they may even reinforce the same mistakes rather than catch them. This makes multi-agent systems fundamentally different from single-agent applications. Looking at each agent independently, or simply checking the final answer, does not tell us whether the collaboration itself worked. The solution is to evaluate what happens between agents. We need to see how information moves through the workflow, how agents hand off results, how shared state changes, and whether different agents actually provide independent reasoning. This article presents a practical approach to evaluating these interactions and using the results to build stronger engineering controls. The goal is not to make LLMs deterministic, but to make their unpredictable behavior visible, measurable, bounded, and recoverable. ## Why agent collaboration needs evals Large language models (LLMs) are inherently nondeterministic. In a multi-agent system, this uncertainty does not disappear. One agent generates information, another agent consumes and interprets it, and its output may then become the context for the next agent. Any falsely generated or interpreted content propagates and amplifies across the entire workflow. Multi-agents are essentially consuming context from one another. We can evaluate it like a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Agent-to-agent interactions can follow the same principles and methodology. A typical RAG pipeline can be decomposed as: User query → retriever → retrieved context (eval) → generation → generated answer (eval) We evaluate content retrieval and generation separately to identify whether the problem originated in retrieval, context quality, or generation. A multi-agent system extends this idea: User query → agent A → handoff → agent B → shared state → agent C → verification → final output Evaluating only the final response — or even evaluating every agent independently — does not tell us whether the collaboration itself worked correctly. We need visibility into what happens between agents. ## Capture the multi-agent execution trace Before evaluating collaboration, we need to observe the complete workflow. Just as LangSmith can capture prompts, retrieved documents, tool calls, and model responses for a RAG application, multi-agent tracing should capture: * Which agents were invoked and in what order * Inputs and outputs of each agent * Agent-to-agent handoff payloads * Routing and delegation decisions * Shared-state reads and updates * Tool calls and results * Retries, loops, and termination decisions * Latency, token usage, and cost at each step The trace effectively becomes the execution history of the multi-agent workflow. Without it, we may know that the final result failed but have little visibility into where the collaboration broke down. ## Evaluate workflow deadlocks and loops Unlike a single-agent application, a multi-agent system is a distributed workflow in which agents depend on one another to decide what happens next. Each agent may wait for information, approval, or an action from another agent. Because these dependencies are often expressed through LLM-driven decisions rather than fixed program logic, the workflow can enter states where no agent can make progress, or where agents repeatedly trigger one another. Deadlocks occur when agents have circular dependencies. For example, an orchestrator waits for a worker agent to return a result, while the worker agent waits for confirmation or additional instructions from the orchestrator. highlights.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Open-Source AI Chatbot Brings Verifiable Answers to Greek Newsrooms ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Open-Source AI Chatbot Brings Verifiable Answers to Greek Newsrooms](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-4258-750x422.png) Open-Source AI Chatbot Brings Verifiable Answers to Greek Newsrooms In an age when misinformation can travel around the world before a correction is even drafted, journalists are increasingly looking for artificial intelligence tools that do more than generate fluent text. They want systems that can prove where every claim came from. A team of Greek researchers has now built exactly that: a fully open-source, retrieval-augmented generation chatbot designed specifically for Greek newsrooms, described in a paper published in the journal SoftwareX. The system answers journalists’ questions using only a curated archive of Greek news articles, attaches citations to every response, and runs entirely on locally deployable components, freeing media organizations from dependence on proprietary cloud platforms. The motivation behind the project is straightforward. Large language models have demonstrated impressive performance on tasks that matter to journalists, including summarization, translation, question answering, and text classification. But general-purpose models rely on knowledge frozen during training, which means their answers can be outdated, unsupported by evidence, or impossible to trace back to a specific source. In a newsroom, where every published claim must be verifiable and attributable, those limitations are disqualifying. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, offers a way around the problem: instead of answering from memory, the model first retrieves relevant documents from a trusted database and then generates a response grounded in that retrieved context, with the sources available for inspection. The new system, developed by Nikolaos Armenakis, Panagiotis Germanakos, Christos Makris, and Constantinos Mourlas, is built entirely from open-source parts. At its core sits Llama-KriKri-8B-Instruct, an instruction-tuned large language model created specifically for Greek, paired with the Multilingual-E5-large-instruct embedding model, which ranks highly on multilingual embedding benchmarks and handles Greek particularly well. The knowledge base consists of roughly 73,000 articles scraped from four major Greek news outlets: kathimerini.gr, efsyn.gr, skai.gr, and zougla.gr. The choice of Greek is deliberate. Despite real progress, Greek natural language processing still lags behind English in available resources, tools, and task coverage, leaving Greek-language newsrooms with few dedicated AI options. The technical pipeline begins with data acquisition and preprocessing. Articles were collected using Beautiful Soup and Selenium, then loaded from CSV files with normalized dates converted into Unix timestamps so that time-based filtering becomes possible. Each document is split into chunks of 500 tokens, the limit imposed by the embedding model, with a 20 percent token overlap between adjacent chunks to preserve semantic continuity and prevent important context from being lost at chunk boundaries. Every chunk receives a unique identifier combining the article’s URL, its row index in the original dataset, and the chunk’s position within the article, guaranteeing that any retrieved fragment can be traced back to its exact origin. The chunks and their metadata, including URL, title, author, website, date, and section, are stored in the open-source Chroma vector database, which was designed to support incremental updates so that newly published articles can be added without rebuilding the entire index. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # Warner’s Agent-Fiduciary Bill Sits in Committee While Two Consumer Agents Enter the Market S. 5051 would bind consumer AI agents to act in their users' best interest. Eighty-one days after introduction its legislative record has one entry, while Muse and GrokBot already hold the authority the bill describes. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| An AI agent can now book your flight, pay for the ticket, and answer the follow-up emails directly inside your private accounts. As these systems gain the ability to initiate transactions and navigate secure environments on your behalf, the core question is whether anything binds them to act in your best interest while they hold that access. While vendors have moved quickly to define their own liability through unilateral contract terms, the only federal legislative effort designed to bind these agents to the user’s best interest remains stalled in the Senate. Senator Mark R. Warner’s S. 5051, the Artificial Intelligence Access, Gatekeeper Exchange, and Nondiscriminatory Transfer Act, was introduced on July 21, 2026. As of October 10, 2026, the bill has sat in the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation for 81 days. Its legislative record is remarkably sparse, showing only a single entry for its introduction. The [official bill page](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/5051) provides the legislative text, while the [tracked legislative record](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/119/s5051) confirms the goal to promote competition and reduce consumer switching costs. The latter record currently assigns the bill a 5% chance of clearing committee and a 2% chance of enactment. Despite the slow pace in Washington, the market has not waited for federal guidance. The urgency of the legislative gap is underscored by the rapid deployment of consumer-facing agents. Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, a system capable of emailing, traveling, and executing payments for users. Earlier, on August 11, 2026, xAI released its GrokBot into beta, a tool that signs into user applications to perform tasks. These deployments highlight a [systemic industry gap](/the-sandbox-is-leaking-metas-muse-containment-failures-reveal-a-systemic-industry-gap/). The liability terms attached to these tools are entirely vendor-defined: Muse offers insured purchase protection capped at $500 per claim, while GrokBot disclaims liability, limiting financial exposure to the greater of fees paid or $100. These figures represent the vendor’s assessment of risk, not a standard of care for the user. S. 5051 proposes a different structural approach. The bill’s stated duties are written operationally: act in the user’s best interest, protect their data, and keep their authority from being handed off without consent. The bill envisions the creation of an FTC registry of trusted, secure AI agents, requires large online platforms to permit authorized agents to act on behalf of users, and allows individuals to designate “Custodial User Agents” to act on their behalf online. The framing has a longer history than the bill itself. Senator Warner’s February 12, 2025 policy agenda, “A Framework for America’s AI Future,” anticipated the legislation with a [fiduciary duty](/glossary/fiduciary-duty-for-ai-agents/) framing, describing its proposed duties as “fiduciary-like.” The June 29, 2026 discussion draft writes those duties as operational requirements: transparency, data protection, and privacy standards. Warner released it that day, and in the [announcement](https://www.warner.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/warner-unveils-discussion-d...

The tip was sent to PhillyUnsolvedMurders, a website used by the department to collect information from the public about unsolved homicide cases. ## Happened During Automated Testing Anthropic notified Philadelphia police about the incident on October 7. According to information the company provided to the department, the model had been testing a random selection of websites when it emailed the false tip. The incident itself happened on July 18. However, Anthropic did not discover it until September 28, after which the company stopped the testing responsible for the submission. The false tip was automatically flagged as spam and was never investigated. ALSO READ [Anthropic Launches Free AI Tool to Find Security Bugs](https://propakistani.pk/2026/10/09/anthropic-launches-free-ai-tool-to-find-security-bugs/) ## Police Systems Were Not Compromised Philadelphia police said there is no indication that the incident resulted in unauthorized access to police systems or any compromise of department data. The department also stressed that all crime tips undergo human review before being passed on for investigative follow-up. Police said tips are treated as leads that must be assessed rather than facts, regardless of who submits them or how they arrive. ALSO READ [AI Giants Need $6 Trillion Revenue to Justify Data Centers](https://propakistani.pk/2026/09/29/ai-giants-need-6-trillion-revenue-to-justify-data-centers/) ## Model May Have Been an Autonomous Agent Based on the details released by police, the model appears to have been operating with some degree of autonomy, although Anthropic has not publicly identified the exact system involved. The incident comes amid growing scrutiny of autonomous AI agents after several recent cases in which models behaved unexpectedly outside their intended environments. Other AI companies, including OpenAI, Meta and Moonshot, have also disclosed incidents involving agents escaping intended restrictions because of sandbox or configuration problems. Anthropic reportedly told Philadelphia police that it planned to publish a report detailing what happened, along with other examples of unintended model behavior. highlights.content: * [United States](/news/us) * / * [Semiconductors](/news/us/semiconductors) * / * NasdaqGS:AVGO # Broadcom (AVGO) Is Leading A $50 Billion AI Chip Debt Push [Simply Wall St](/news/about-simply-wall-st-news) Reviewed by[Bailey](/community/users/fxenyjkf) * Broadcom (NasdaqGS:AVGO) is leading a planned US$50b debt financing package for OpenAI's Nexus custom AI chip buildout, disclosed on 9 October 2026. * The financing push targets large scale AI infrastructure, as OpenAI seeks dedicated chip capacity beyond general purpose GPU supply. * Sector peers such as Oracle and SpaceX are also pursuing multibillion dollar funding deals to secure next generation chip manufacturing and data center resources. * Broadcom's role in organising US$50b of debt for OpenAI's Nexus chips is only part of the funding story now reshaping AI credit markets. We have also spotted [1 warning sign](https://simplywall.st/stocks/us/semiconductors/nasdaq-avgo/broadcom) worth knowing about at Broadcom. To put this Broadcom move in context, explore other AI infrastructure plays through [92 AI infrastructure stocks](https://simplywall.st/discover/investing-ideas/473744/ai-infrastructure-stocks/global). NasdaqGS:AVGO 1-Year Stock Price Chart Broadcom designs and supplies semiconductor hardware and infrastructure software, which puts it directly in the flow of capital rushing into AI data centers and custom chip projects like Nexus. Its role as a large US firm with a US$1.7b market cap helps it act as a coordination point for complex financing tied to that buildout. See [how Broadcom's balance sheet measures up](https://simplywall.st/stocks/us/semiconductors/nasdaq-avgo/broadcom/health). Advertisement ### Broadcom takes on more AI financing risk to deepen revenue visibility For Broadcom, organizing US$50b of debt for OpenAI’s Nexus chips leans into the existing narrative that AI revenue visibility is strengthening while financing risk is becoming the real test. The move supports the bull case catalyst of multi year AI semiconductor demand from hyperscalers and reinforces the idea that Broadcom is central to large custom XPU deployments. At the same time, it adds weight to the bear side that already flags AI XPV structures and off balance sheet exposure as key risks, because another large financing layer ties Broadcom more tightly to a small group of AI customers and to residual value assumptions on high cost hardware. See how these catalysts shape [Broadcom's path to a $532 fair value](https://simplywall.st/narratives/4555lmi3-avgo-upcoming-ai-chip-production-with-key-partner-will-shape-competitive-position). The clearest signpost from here is how Broadcom frames its AI XPV commitments and residual value guarantees at the next detailed quarterly report. This includes any updated figures on maximum exposure versus free cash flow and whether consolidated gross margin guidance reflects the added mix of financed, lower margin AI XPUs. AI Agents.titleZh: AI agents can be unpredictable. Your control layer shouldn't be. | VentureBeat
AI Agents.content: # AI agents can be unpredictable. Your control layer shouldn't be. In multi-agent systems, agents can be individually correct and still produce a wrong result when they work together. One agent’s output becomes another agent’s context. Information can be lost or misinterpreted during a handoff, shared state can drift, and agents can get stuck in loops or deadlocks. When several agents rely on the same underlying model, they may even reinforce the same mistakes rather than catch them. This makes multi-agent systems fundamentally different from single-agent applications. Looking at each agent independently, or simply checking the final answer, does not tell us whether the collaboration itself worked. The solution is to evaluate what happens between agents. We need to see how information moves through the workflow, how agents hand off results, how shared state changes, and whether different agents actually provide independent reasoning. This article presents a practical approach to evaluating these interactions and using the results to build stronger engineering controls. The goal is not to make LLMs deterministic, but to make their unpredictable behavior visible, measurable, bounded, and recoverable. ## Why agent collaboration needs evals Large language models (LLMs) are inherently nondeterministic. In a multi-agent system, this uncertainty does not disappear. One agent generates information, another agent consumes and interprets it, and its output may then become the context for the next agent. Any falsely generated or interpreted content propagates and amplifies across the entire workflow. Multi-agents are essentially consuming context from one another. We can evaluate it like a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Agent-to-agent interactions can follow the same principles and methodology. A typical RAG pipeline can be decomposed as: User query → retriever → retrieved context (eval) → generation → generated answer (eval) We evaluate content retrieval and generation separately to identify whether the problem originated in retrieval, context quality, or generation. A multi-agent system extends this idea: User query → agent A → handoff → agent B → shared state → agent C → verification → final output Evaluating only the final response — or even evaluating every agent independently — does not tell us whether the collaboration itself worked correctly. We need visibility into what happens between agents. ## Capture the multi-agent execution trace Before evaluating collaboration, we need to observe the complete workflow. Just as LangSmith can capture prompts, retrieved documents, tool calls, and model responses for a RAG application, multi-agent tracing should capture: * Which agents were invoked and in what order * Inputs and outputs of each agent * Agent-to-agent handoff payloads * Routing and delegation decisions * Shared-state reads and updates * Tool calls and results * Retries, loops, and termination decisions * Latency, token usage, and cost at each step The trace effectively becomes the execution history of the multi-agent workflow. Without it, we may know that the final result failed but have little visibility into where the collaboration broke down. ## Evaluate workflow deadlocks and loops Unlike a single-agent application, a multi-agent system is a distributed workflow in which agents depend on one another to decide what happens next. Each agent may wait for information, approval, or an action from another agent. Because these dependencies are often expressed through LLM-driven decisions rather than fixed program logic, the workflow can enter states where no agent can make progress, or where agents repeatedly trigger one another. Deadlocks occur when agents have circular dependencies. For example, an orchestrator waits for a worker agent to return a result, while the worker agent waits for confirmation or additional instructions from the orchestrator. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # Warner’s Agent-Fiduciary Bill Sits in Committee While Two Consumer Agents Enter the Market S. 5051 would bind consumer AI agents to act in their users' best interest. Eighty-one days after introduction its legislative record has one entry, while Muse and GrokBot already hold the authority the bill describes. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| An AI agent can now book your flight, pay for the ticket, and answer the follow-up emails directly inside your private accounts. As these systems gain the ability to initiate transactions and navigate secure environments on your behalf, the core question is whether anything binds them to act in your best interest while they hold that access. While vendors have moved quickly to define their own liability through unilateral contract terms, the only federal legislative effort designed to bind these agents to the user’s best interest remains stalled in the Senate. Senator Mark R. Warner’s S. 5051, the Artificial Intelligence Access, Gatekeeper Exchange, and Nondiscriminatory Transfer Act, was introduced on July 21, 2026. As of October 10, 2026, the bill has sat in the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation for 81 days. Its legislative record is remarkably sparse, showing only a single entry for its introduction. The [official bill page](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/5051) provides the legislative text, while the [tracked legislative record](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/119/s5051) confirms the goal to promote competition and reduce consumer switching costs. The latter record currently assigns the bill a 5% chance of clearing committee and a 2% chance of enactment. Despite the slow pace in Washington, the market has not waited for federal guidance. The urgency of the legislative gap is underscored by the rapid deployment of consumer-facing agents. Meta launched Muse on September 8, 2026, a system capable of emailing, traveling, and executing payments for users. Earlier, on August 11, 2026, xAI released its GrokBot into beta, a tool that signs into user applications to perform tasks. These deployments highlight a [systemic industry gap](/the-sandbox-is-leaking-metas-muse-containment-failures-reveal-a-systemic-industry-gap/). The liability terms attached to these tools are entirely vendor-defined: Muse offers insured purchase protection capped at $500 per claim, while GrokBot disclaims liability, limiting financial exposure to the greater of fees paid or $100. These figures represent the vendor’s assessment of risk, not a standard of care for the user. S. 5051 proposes a different structural approach. The bill’s stated duties are written operationally: act in the user’s best interest, protect their data, and keep their authority from being handed off without consent. The bill envisions the creation of an FTC registry of trusted, secure AI agents, requires large online platforms to permit authorized agents to act on behalf of users, and allows individuals to designate “Custodial User Agents” to act on their behalf online. The framing has a longer history than the bill itself. Senator Warner’s February 12, 2025 policy agenda, “A Framework for America’s AI Future,” anticipated the legislation with a [fiduciary duty](/glossary/fiduciary-duty-for-ai-agents/) framing, describing its proposed duties as “fiduciary-like.” The June 29, 2026 discussion draft writes those duties as operational requirements: transparency, data protection, and privacy standards. The tip was sent to PhillyUnsolvedMurders, a website used by the department to collect information from the public about unsolved homicide cases. ## Happened During Automated Testing Anthropic notified Philadelphia police about the incident on October 7. According to information the company provided to the department, the model had been testing a random selection of websites when it emailed the false tip. The incident itself happened on July 18. However, Anthropic did not discover it until September 28, after which the company stopped the testing responsible for the submission. The false tip was automatically flagged as spam and was never investigated. The incident comes amid growing scrutiny of autonomous AI agents after several recent cases in which models behaved unexpectedly outside their intended environments. Other AI companies, including OpenAI, Meta and Moonshot, have also disclosed incidents involving agents escaping intended restrictions because of sandbox or configuration problems. Anthropic reportedly told Philadelphia police that it planned to publish a report detailing what happened, along with other examples of unintended model behavior. AI Agents.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Google Unveils Enterprise Gemini Agent—"An AI Colleague with Its Own Email Account" [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Google has unveiled an enterprise-grade Gemini agent designed to function as an autonomous AI colleague within organizations. The agent is assigned its own Workspace account and email address, enabling it to understand organizational context—including team structures, time zones, approval hierarchies, and calendars—and to plan and execute work toward assigned goals. It integrates with a wide range of enterprise tools including Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, BigQuery, Databricks, and Snowflake, and supports external AI models such as Anthropic's Claude. The announcement comes as Google Cloud reported Q2 revenue of $24.8 billion, up 82% year-over-year, far outpacing Alphabet's search segment growth of 17%. Approximately 90% of Fortune 100 companies now use Gemini Enterprise tools, and Gemini's monthly active users have surpassed 1 billion. ##### Key Elements ![Google Unveils Enterprise Gemini Agent—](https://img.biggo.com/HzBmqePsgl-GDbYtSYGkaoQsZazV5abkfIqeV1sodVE/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzdiNDJiMzBhLTJkMjktNDczYi04NWYwLThhNjNmOGJjMjJlYl8xNzkxNjgyNzkwX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Google has expanded its Gemini AI chatbot into a service that connects to enterprise internal systems, handling everything from work planning to execution. The newly unveiled enterprise agent is distinguished by its ability to receive its own Workspace account and email address—just like a human employee—allowing it to understand organizational work context and perform tasks autonomously. Google Cloud unveiled the Gemini-based unified agent at the "Gemini at Work 2026" event, which ran through the 8th. The company plans to offer it to enterprise customers first, then expand to general consumers. The agent's core differentiator is that it goes beyond simply executing individual instructions—it plans and executes entire workstreams aligned with assigned goals. It autonomously leverages customized functions and tools needed to achieve objectives, connecting to enterprise internal systems to carry out tasks. The agent is assigned a Google Workspace account and email address identical to those of employees. Through this, it understands work context by identifying team memberships, time zones, approval authorities, and calendar schedules. Users can invoke the agent by tagging it, sending emails, sharing materials, or adding it to group chat rooms. Transparency features allow users to monitor the agent's work process. In the "Task Inbox," users can review the agent's processing steps, sub-agent task delegation, requested functions and code, and progress status. When tasks are executed, audit logs explicitly identify the agent—not a human—as the executing entity. A key strength is the ability to connect to a wide range of enterprise work tools and data systems. Beyond Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, and Confluence, the agent integrates with BigQuery, Databricks, PostgreSQL, and Snowflake. It also supports secure connections to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers both inside and outside corporate networks. Users can attach files and folders to work requests, or bundle files and functions needed for specific tasks into projects. The agent operates on iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, and also runs via command-line interfaces and platforms like ServiceNow. The AI model used for agent tasks is automatically selected by the system by default, but users can choose manually. Google Cloud is supporting external model selection starting with Anthropic's Claude, with plans to expand to open-source and private models in the future. C...

LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [AI & Machine Learning](https://shattered.io/ai-machine-learning/) # TypeSafe AI’s Jev Hits $7.5B Valuation in Weeks [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/emarchetti.webp) [Dr. Elena Marchetti](https://shattered.io/author/emarchetti/) Updated Oct 10, 2026 · 13 min read A startup most people had never heard of a month ago just got valued higher than most publicly traded software companies. TypeSafe AI, the maker of a non-text AI model called Jev, has raised $870 million in a new funding round that values the company at $7.5 billion, according to reporting from TechCrunch, Reuters, and Bloomberg (via Investing.com). The round, led by Andreessen Horowitz with participation from Sequoia and existing backer DCVC, lands just weeks after Jev’s public debut, and it’s forcing a fresh conversation about what “AI model” even means in 2026. The headline number is eye-catching on its own. What makes it stranger is the product behind it. Jev isn’t a chatbot, doesn’t write essays, and won’t draft your emails. It doesn’t output text at all. Instead, built on a transformer architecture, it produces probabilities, what TypeSafe AI calls “calibrated decisions.” That’s a deliberate departure from the [large language model](https://shattered.io/category/ai-machine-learning/) playbook that has dominated AI headlines since ChatGPT’s debut, and investors are betting real money that the departure is the point. ## What TypeSafe AI and Jev Actually Are TypeSafe AI was founded in 2024 by three people with resumes that read like a checklist of the industry’s biggest labs. Diogo Almeida previously worked as a researcher at OpenAI. Sasha Sheng came from a research engineering role at Meta. Erik Gafni rounds out the founding team as an engineer and entrepreneur, according to the company’s own announcement. Two years later, the trio shipped Jev, and the launch video reportedly went viral fast enough to pull in a wave of interest from chief executives, developers, and investors almost overnight. Almeida described that moment plainly. “The launch video going viral led to a surge of interest from chief executives, developers, and investors,” he said, a comment that captures how quickly a niche technical demo turned into a boardroom conversation. The distinction that TypeSafe AI keeps pressing is that Jev is explicitly not a large language model. It doesn’t generate the next token in a sentence. It evaluates inputs and returns a probability-weighted decision, the kind of output a fraud-detection system, a logistics router, or a pricing engine might need far more than a paragraph of prose. That framing matters because it positions Jev against a different competitive set than [GPT-6](https://shattered.io/gpt-6-intelligent-ui-chatgpt-rollout-2026/) or [Claude Opus 5.5](https://shattered.io/claude-opus-5-5-beats-gpt-5-6-sol-benchmark-2026/). Those systems compete on reasoning depth, context windows, and conversational nuance. Jev, as described by TypeSafe AI, competes on speed and cost for narrow, structured decisions, the unglamorous but high-volume work that sits behind a lot of enterprise software. ## The $870 Million Round, Broken Down The size of the round alone puts TypeSafe AI in rarefied company for a startup barely two years old. Andreessen Horowitz led the investment, with Sequoia joining as a new backer alongside DCVC, which had already invested in an earlier round, per the company’s statement. None of the three firms are strangers to swinging big on AI infrastructure bets, but a16z’s decision to lead here is notable given how selective the firm has been about which foundation-model companies it backs directly versus through its broader portfolio. LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Open-Source AI Chatbot Brings Verifiable Answers to Greek Newsrooms ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Open-Source AI Chatbot Brings Verifiable Answers to Greek Newsrooms](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-4258-750x422.png) Open-Source AI Chatbot Brings Verifiable Answers to Greek Newsrooms In an age when misinformation can travel around the world before a correction is even drafted, journalists are increasingly looking for artificial intelligence tools that do more than generate fluent text. They want systems that can prove where every claim came from. A team of Greek researchers has now built exactly that: a fully open-source, retrieval-augmented generation chatbot designed specifically for Greek newsrooms, described in a paper published in the journal SoftwareX. The system answers journalists’ questions using only a curated archive of Greek news articles, attaches citations to every response, and runs entirely on locally deployable components, freeing media organizations from dependence on proprietary cloud platforms. The motivation behind the project is straightforward. Large language models have demonstrated impressive performance on tasks that matter to journalists, including summarization, translation, question answering, and text classification. But general-purpose models rely on knowledge frozen during training, which means their answers can be outdated, unsupported by evidence, or impossible to trace back to a specific source. In a newsroom, where every published claim must be verifiable and attributable, those limitations are disqualifying. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, offers a way around the problem: instead of answering from memory, the model first retrieves relevant documents from a trusted database and then generates a response grounded in that retrieved context, with the sources available for inspection. The new system, developed by Nikolaos Armenakis, Panagiotis Germanakos, Christos Makris, and Constantinos Mourlas, is built entirely from open-source parts. At its core sits Llama-KriKri-8B-Instruct, an instruction-tuned large language model created specifically for Greek, paired with the Multilingual-E5-large-instruct embedding model, which ranks highly on multilingual embedding benchmarks and handles Greek particularly well. The knowledge base consists of roughly 73,000 articles scraped from four major Greek news outlets: kathimerini.gr, efsyn.gr, skai.gr, and zougla.gr. The choice of Greek is deliberate. Despite real progress, Greek natural language processing still lags behind English in available resources, tools, and task coverage, leaving Greek-language newsrooms with few dedicated AI options. The technical pipeline begins with data acquisition and preprocessing. Articles were collected using Beautiful Soup and Selenium, then loaded from CSV files with normalized dates converted into Unix timestamps so that time-based filtering becomes possible. Each document is split into chunks of 500 tokens, the limit imposed by the embedding model, with a 20 percent token overlap between adjacent chunks to preserve semantic continuity and prevent important context from being lost at chunk boundaries. Every chunk receives a unique identifier combining the article’s URL, its row index in the original dataset, and the chunk’s position within the article, guaranteeing that any retrieved fragment can be traced back to its exact origin. The chunks and their metadata, including URL, title, author, website, date, and section, are stored in the open-source Chroma vector database, which was designed to support incremental updates so that newly published articles can be added without rebuilding the entire index. LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # AI Tumor Board Passes Reproducibility Test: Structured Output Tames Sarcoma LLM Chaos ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![AI Tumor Board Passes Reproducibility Test: Structured Output Tames Sarcoma LLM Chaos](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-4303-750x422.png) AI Tumor Board Passes Reproducibility Test: Structured Output Tames Sarcoma LLM Chaos Artificial intelligence has been edging closer to the rooms where cancer treatment decisions are made, but a stubborn problem has kept it at arm’s length: when you ask a large language model the same clinical question twice, you do not always get the same answer. Now a team at University Hospital Schleswig-Holstein in Lübeck, Germany, reports that a carefully engineered framework can make an AI’s tumor-board recommendations almost perfectly repeatable. In a study published in Scientific Reports, the researchers simulated multidisciplinary sarcoma tumor boards using the Claude Opus 4.5 model and found that 94 percent of its decision codes were identical across repeated runs of the same case — a dramatic improvement over the roughly 20 percent consistency documented in earlier, free-form benchmarks. The stakes are higher than they might sound. Sarcomas, a family of more than 100 rare connective-tissue cancers, are among the most demanding cases any tumor board faces. Decisions about biopsy route, surgical margins, reconstruction, radiotherapy and chemotherapy must be woven together, and early missteps can cost patients a limb, a function, or a cure. Previous studies testing language models against human boards in sarcoma were sobering: in a benchmark against 21 European sarcoma centers, models including GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet showed consistency in only one in five cases, and their best alignment with human consensus reached just 60 percent. Worse, the models occasionally invented guideline citations and fabricated survival statistics — the notorious hallucination problem — with explicit guideline derivation identifiable in fewer than half of responses. The German team, led by Tekoshin Ammo and Moritz Englich of the Department of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgery, attacked the problem architecturally rather than with better pleading. Their framework forces the model to return its answers through a tool-use interface as structured JSON data, validated at run time against a schema defined in the Python library Pydantic. The schema covers 21 individual decision codes across nine clinical domains — imaging, staging, surgical strategy, margin goals, reconstruction, functional reconstruction, radiotherapy strategy and dose, and systemic therapy. Categorical fields are locked to controlled vocabularies: the model cannot choose between “wide local excision” and “definitive surgical excision,” because only the enumerated value wide\_excision passes validation. Inference was run at temperature 0.0, the setting that suppresses random sampling and pushes the model toward its most probable output. On top of the schema, the system prompt layered seven coordinated prompting techniques, including role prompting, rule-based prompting, negative prompting, and conditional-logic rules that couple decisions to one another — for instance, instructing the model to record “none” for first-line chemotherapy when the overall systemic-therapy decision is negative. Two semantic clarifications resolved ambiguities that had plagued earlier iterations: whether a “True” for an imaging recommendation meant the scan still needed to be performed or merely belonged to the recommended workup, and whether a functional-reconstruction flag referred to a procedure definitively planned. LLMs.titleZh: Newer AI Models Missed More Payment Fraud in Coinbase Benchmark | TokenPost
LLMs.content: [![TOKENPOST](/tokenpost-logo.svg)](/) 2 min read [![](/google-g.png)Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=tokenpost.com) # Newer AI Models Missed More Payment Fraud in Coinbase Benchmark A fixed replay of 16,140 Onramp transactions found lower fraud coverage for Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 (sol), despite GPT-5.6’s higher precision. ![](https://f1.tokenpost.com/2024/11/9vga9k0r6d.png) By **[Simon Yoon](/reporters/26)** Published ![Payment terminal beside blank cards under cool studio light / TokenPost.ai](https://mzwrodgsdjfdyvnraeya.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/article-media/articles/ce638629354e718dc2bd9bc53452b94fb1a49d1d327498b420e4b3dd99948fee.webp) Payment terminal beside blank cards under cool studio light / TokenPost.ai In a controlled replay of Coinbase Onramp activity, updated models from three major AI families caught a smaller share of fraudulent payments than the versions they replaced, highlighting potential risks from upgrades in specialized detection systems. The evaluation covered 16,140 transactions involving 7,293 users, including 813 confirmed fraudulent transactions. Each model was tested against the same transaction group, contextual-review process and risk-to-decision policy. Across the comparisons, Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 (sol) posted lower recall, F1 and dollar-weighted recall than the earlier versions. Recall measures the share of fraudulent transactions detected, while dollar-weighted recall measures the share of fraudulent transaction value identified. Opus 5’s recall declined by 0.8 percentage points compared with Opus 4.5. It also posted lower precision, F1 and dollar-weighted recall, although the other changes were not quantified. Sonnet 5’s recall fell by 22.2 percentage points, and its dollar-weighted recall dropped by 22.9 percentage points. Precision also declined. GPT-5.6 (sol) produced a different trade-off against GPT-5.4. Its precision rose by 11.5 percentage points, while recall fell by 20.7 percentage points and dollar-weighted recall declined by 21.8 percentage points. F1 also fell. “Newer LLMs are not necessarily better at domain-specific tasks,” Yao Ma and Xuwei Tan wrote. The benchmark showed a regression but did not establish its cause. Possible explanations included changed decision boundaries, post-training trade-offs and different training-data mixtures. None was assigned as the reason for the results. The test replayed nine weeks of production data collected before the risk agent was rolled out. It did not compare live customer outcomes or establish a specific amount of customer losses caused by the model changes. Coinbase Onramp allows users to buy crypto through partner applications, including guest checkout. Its risk system combines a traditional machine-learning model and rules engine with selective large language model review of recent transaction behavior. A separate evaluation published Oct. 8, 2026, found that a post-trained Qwen3.5-9B model exceeded Opus 4.5 on all four fraud metrics. The model posted gains of 7.5 percentage points in precision, 12.0 percentage points in recall, 9.6 percentage points in F1 and 35.4 percentage points in dollar-weighted recall. Detection quality and speed were measured separately. Online serving tests recorded P50 end-to-end large language model request latency of 0.683 seconds for the system versus 1.515 seconds for Opus 4.5. ![](https://f1.tokenpost.com/2024/11/9vga9k0r6d.png) ## Simon Yoon Reporter Simon Yoon reports on blockchain technology for TokenPost. DeepL’s next-generation LLM engine, Google’s Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, and OpenAI’s newly discounted GPT-6 Sol and Luna models are no longer just competing on vocabulary size. They are competing on context windows, audio latency, and per-character pricing that shifts by the month as three of the largest AI labs in the world treat translation as a byproduct of their flagship model releases rather than a dedicated product line. For any Canadian team juggling English and French content under Quebec’s Bill 96, federal bilingual publishing rules, or just a national customer base that expects service in both official languages, picking the wrong AI translator can mean paying three times more per million characters than necessary or shipping a product description that reads like it was run through a machine translation engine from a decade ago. This comparison breaks down **DeepL, Google Translate (now powered largely by Gemini), and ChatGPT** as AI translator options for Canadian teams heading into the final months of 2026: what each model actually is right now, what it costs down to the dollar, how it benchmarks against independently published scores, and which one fits specific real-world jobs ranging from bilingual legal contracts to live customer support chat. We’ll also cover the two questions most comparison articles skip entirely: how each tool handles Canadian French specifically, and where your translated text actually goes once you hit submit. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. OpenAI cut GPT-6 Sol’s API pricing in half on October 7, 2026, dropping input costs from $4 to $2 per million tokens and output from $20 to $10 per million tokens, while simultaneously introducing GPT-6 Luna as a budget-tier model explicitly built for high-volume tasks like translation and summarization rather than complex reasoning. That is a meaningful shift for any business running translation at scale through an API, since token costs on long documents compound quickly. Days earlier, Alibaba’s QwenCloud division pushed out Qwen3.8-LiveTranslate-Flash-Realtime, a simultaneous audio and video translation model covering 60 source languages with voice output in 29 languages, signalling that the translation race now includes major Chinese AI labs as serious contenders rather than just the familiar Western incumbents most Canadian IT buyers default to. The AI solution support program assists with tasks needed to prepare for a startup—such as market research, content creation, and service development—to turn participants' ideas into actual products and services. The providers and solutions will be released on the 12th. The focus was on quality so participants can easily choose and actually use the solutions needed in the startup process. An evaluation committee of AI and software technology experts used the applicant solutions and reviewed their versatility, the appropriateness of technology and price, and security. The selected solutions help with tasks needed to prepare for a startup, from building websites to generating promotional content and drafting contracts. Participants can build websites that introduce their products and services with AI or produce product images and promotional content to turn their ideas into deliverables. This is expected to ease the burden of startup preparation and refine and develop participants' ideas. The AI solution list can be found on the "Startup for All platform." Key functions and how to use each solution can be checked from the 14th. Those advancing to round 1 of the second "Startup for All" can use AI solutions with a per-person limit of 1 million won. Starting on the 16th, applicants can select the necessary solutions on the platform and apply to use them. The Ministry of SMEs and Startups (MSS) will also strengthen usage guidance so participants can easily grasp each solution's functions and purpose. It plans to provide explanatory videos for each solution to help compare and choose services and use them effectively for startup preparation. AI Product.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [AI & Machine Learning](https://shattered.io/ai-machine-learning/) # TypeSafe AI’s Jev Hits $7.5B Valuation in Weeks [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/emarchetti.webp) [Dr. Elena Marchetti](https://shattered.io/author/emarchetti/) Updated Oct 10, 2026 · 13 min read A startup most people had never heard of a month ago just got valued higher than most publicly traded software companies. TypeSafe AI, the maker of a non-text AI model called Jev, has raised $870 million in a new funding round that values the company at $7.5 billion, according to reporting from TechCrunch, Reuters, and Bloomberg (via Investing.com). The round, led by Andreessen Horowitz with participation from Sequoia and existing backer DCVC, lands just weeks after Jev’s public debut, and it’s forcing a fresh conversation about what “AI model” even means in 2026. The headline number is eye-catching on its own. What makes it stranger is the product behind it. Jev isn’t a chatbot, doesn’t write essays, and won’t draft your emails. It doesn’t output text at all. Instead, built on a transformer architecture, it produces probabilities, what TypeSafe AI calls “calibrated decisions.” That’s a deliberate departure from the [large language model](https://shattered.io/category/ai-machine-learning/) playbook that has dominated AI headlines since ChatGPT’s debut, and investors are betting real money that the departure is the point. ## What TypeSafe AI and Jev Actually Are TypeSafe AI was founded in 2024 by three people with resumes that read like a checklist of the industry’s biggest labs. Diogo Almeida previously worked as a researcher at OpenAI. Sasha Sheng came from a research engineering role at Meta. Erik Gafni rounds out the founding team as an engineer and entrepreneur, according to the company’s own announcement. Two years later, the trio shipped Jev, and the launch video reportedly went viral fast enough to pull in a wave of interest from chief executives, developers, and investors almost overnight. Almeida described that moment plainly. “The launch video going viral led to a surge of interest from chief executives, developers, and investors,” he said, a comment that captures how quickly a niche technical demo turned into a boardroom conversation. The distinction that TypeSafe AI keeps pressing is that Jev is explicitly not a large language model. It doesn’t generate the next token in a sentence. It evaluates inputs and returns a probability-weighted decision, the kind of output a fraud-detection system, a logistics router, or a pricing engine might need far more than a paragraph of prose. That framing matters because it positions Jev against a different competitive set than [GPT-6](https://shattered.io/gpt-6-intelligent-ui-chatgpt-rollout-2026/) or [Claude Opus 5.5](https://shattered.io/claude-opus-5-5-beats-gpt-5-6-sol-benchmark-2026/). Those systems compete on reasoning depth, context windows, and conversational nuance. Jev, as described by TypeSafe AI, competes on speed and cost for narrow, structured decisions, the unglamorous but high-volume work that sits behind a lot of enterprise software. ## The $870 Million Round, Broken Down The size of the round alone puts TypeSafe AI in rarefied company for a startup barely two years old. Andreessen Horowitz led the investment, with Sequoia joining as a new backer alongside DCVC, which had already invested in an earlier round, per the company’s statement. None of the three firms are strangers to swinging big on AI infrastructure bets, but a16z’s decision to lead here is notable given how selective the firm has been about which foundation-model companies it backs directly versus through its broader portfolio. Open Source AI.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Peter Werry Says the Hard Part of AI Retrieval Isn't the LLM — It's the Scaffolding [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Unblocked's Peter Werry argues that the retrieval layer most AI agents rely on — semantic RAG over documents and code — handles only half the problem. The other half, structured queries over institutional data, is where the real engineering difficulty sits. In a demonstration, attaching Unblocked's context engine to a Claude task cut cost from $2.60 to $1.29 and time from three minutes to 90 seconds. But Werry's central claim is contrarian: generating the database query is the easy part. The hard part is the scaffolding around it — schema discovery, identity resolution, validation, and self-correction. He walks through each layer, showing that deterministic procedural methods outperform LLM-first approaches for structured tasks. The talk closes with two open-source projects that let teams test the approach without committing to Unblocked's hosted product. ##### Key Elements ![Peter Werry Says the Hard Part of AI Retrieval Isn't the LLM — It's the Scaffolding](https://img.biggo.com/-miGIMKE9EIEgY8qz9j426WlO6XXrEs3SN8g-LmpKmk/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzMyODA0ZGY3NTgwMDlhZTNfMTc5MTY2ODM3OF9jb3Zlci5qcGc.webp) ### The Context Layer Problem Before AI agents, "you were the context layer," Peter Werry told the audience at the AI Engineer conference. A new employee had to read the codebase, dig through documentation systems, and absorb the shared history built up through incidents and "the battle scars that come with it." That absorption process is now being automated. Werry, a speaker from Unblocked, frames the pre-agent era bluntly: humans were the institutional context layer. A context engine automates that absorption, taking scattered context in and emitting grounded context out — interrelated, intent-specific, personalized, and permissions-aware. He demonstrated the difference with a Claude session. Asked to create a plan to optimize a component in Unblocked's SourceMark engine without a context engine, Claude behaves "like a new employee" — it "reps around your code base" trying to figure out what's going on, and eventually "confidently projects that it's figured it out." With the context engine attached, Claude calls the engine, which returns a task-specific context bundle referencing source code plus Notion architecture documents, pull requests, and Slack conversations about optimizing that component. The bundle includes links so Claude can fetch more if needed. The measured result: | Metric | Without context engine | With context engine | | --- | --- | --- | | Cost | Up to $2.60 | $1.29 | | Time | Up to 3 minutes | ~1 minute 30 seconds | | Reduction | — | ~50% cost | Werry calls the 50% cost reduction "pretty incredible." It's worth noting this is a single comparison he ran, not a benchmark across tasks. ### Two Halves of Retrieval The most vivid proof that structured queries matter came from a real regression hunt. Werry's colleague Richie, who works on Unblocked's code review product, noticed the number of issues the product surfaced was dropping. He asked Unblocked, which narrowed it quickly to a likely cause: the team had switched from Opus 4.6 to Opus 4.8, and the behavioral characteristics behind the scenes caused the issue count to drop. Richie then asked Unblocked to fix it, and it created a PR behind the scenes. Werry highlights the PR description as the striking part: it understood the PR that caused the regression in the first place, found a Slack conversation where the issue was discussed, and pulled data from it to inform the fix. He calls this "just nuts." The methodological point matters more than the anecdote. Rich...

Open Source AI.titleZh: Microsoft leans on open weight model from Chinese AI lab to challenge Jev
Open Source AI.content: ai and ml # Microsoft leans on open weight model from Chinese AI lab to challenge Jev The first version of Microsoft-Decision-1 is based on Qwen3.5-9B, but the next will sport homegrown tech, Redmond reassures ### READ MORE * #### Microsoft 365 subscribers set to lose up to 4 TB of OneDrive storage * #### US Navy bets another $150M on fighter drone that skips the runway * #### Microsoft and Anthropic play invoice tennis with startup's $17,600 Claude bill * #### India’s tech giants shrug off changes to USA’s skilled visa program * #### There can be only one: Google Cloud casts Gemini as your enterprise AI hero Microsoft has joined the Jev fan club, an accidental group of companies that share a common desire to be recognized for their own decision models. Jev, announced by TypeSafe AI three weeks ago, is a large language model (LLM) tuned to respond to certain types of questions with a limited range of responses, rated by probability. Due to its speed, relative affordability, and response constraints, it's well-suited for a variety of business applications where open-ended text of uncertain accuracy might be undesirable. One of the selling points of Jev is that decision models don't hallucinate in the way that standard LLMs do. But decision models can make errors and their popularity has already prompted researchers to explore how those errors might be magnified. Nonetheless, they have their uses. The attention lavished on Jev prompted other companies to declare that they too have decision models to offer, even though machine learning researchers have long been able to create classifier models for probability-based decisions. OpenAI said its Decisions API has entered public beta. Cloudflare chimed in with its Clef model. Strands trotted out Strands Decider 2B, "a small, open source, decision model." Liquid AI introduced d1. Perplexity launched its Decisions API. Snowflake talked up its own decision model. Then there's Surogate Rune and H2O.ai's H2O-Lightning-4B, a decision model built on Qwen3.5-4B. All told, more than 100 such models are now vying for attention. Now it's Microsoft's turn. "Decision models are quickly emerging as an important new category in AI," said Achint Srivastava, VP of software engineering in the Office of the CTO at Microsoft, in a blog post on Friday. "Unlike LLMs, which are designed to generate text or reason through complex problems, decision models are purpose-built to deliver structured outputs that software can immediately act on. And once you understand that capability – making decisions and classifying things at very low cost with high performance – all kinds of useful tasks get unlocked." Microsoft's entrant into the race is called Microsoft-Decision-1, which is offered via Microsoft Foundry and, soon, via OpenRouter. Redmond's decision model, like H2O's, is based on a Qwen model, Qwen3.5-9B in this instance. The Qwen model family is developed by Alibaba Cloud, the cloud computing arm of Chinese tech giant Alibaba. Microsoft, for reasons not disclosed, said it will soon rebase the Decision-1 on its models and those from OpenAI. The US software giant claims its model is 2.5x faster than H2O-Lightning-4B and 2.8x faster than Jev in its latency test, leads the pack in accuracy (83.5 percent) on 36 benchmarks, ranks second (behind Quyet-1.0-Large) in confidence score (92.2 percent), and is more than 20x cheaper than OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol in text classification tasks. Input tokens cost $0.042 per million tokens and output tokens are free. "Now that agentic AI is a reality, we’ve seen that cost plays a major role in how people decide to use AI," said Srivastava. "And it’s increasingly important to choose the right model for the right job." ®

On October 6, 2026, the company published 722 preprints to a public GitHub repository, each one claiming progress on one of 372 unsolved or hard mathematical problems, generated with help from an internal mathematical-reasoning system. By October 7, three of those manuscripts were gone, pulled after a sign error in a single proof cascaded through two other papers that depended on it. Retraction Watch broke the story on October 8, and by October 10 the episode had become a case study in what happens when a frontier AI lab treats mathematics releases like software releases: ship fast, patch faster. The story matters beyond mathematics departments. OpenAI’s [math dump](https://tech-insider.org/openai-377-vs-372-math-results-one-prompt-2026/) was widely read as a signal of how close large language models are to doing original research, not just passing benchmarks. The 24-hour retraction is now the clearest evidence yet of the gap between a model producing plausible-looking proofs at scale and a result the mathematical community can actually trust. [Tbreak Editor](https://tbreak.com/author/tbreak/) Change language to 0:00 Nvidia plans to invest in d-Matrix, an AI inference chip startup that sells processors which compete with its own, according to [The Information](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/nvidia-invest-chip-rival-d-matrix-challengers-choose-partnership). Citing three people with knowledge of the deal, the report says the investment is part of a push to make Nvidia’s technology work with chips from other designers. Neither Nvidia nor d-Matrix has confirmed it, and they haven’t disclosed the size or timing. The reported stake would follow similar arrangements with Marvell, Intel and Amazon. Nvidia and Marvell announced a [strategic partnership](https://investor.nvidia.com/news/press-release-details/2026/NVIDIA-AI-Ecosystem-Expands-as-Marvell-Joins-Forces-Through-NVLink-Fusion/) on 31 March that connects Marvell’s custom chips to Nvidia’s AI factory ecosystem through NVLink Fusion, and Nvidia has said it also invested in Marvell. AWS, meanwhile, [said in December](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/aws-integrates-ai-infrastructure-with-nvidia-nvlink-fusion-for-trainium4-deployment/) that it is designing its Trainium4 chips to work with NVLink Fusion. ## Subscribe to our Newsletters for more Business Stories Found us on Google? [Add tbreak as a preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=tbreak.com) to see more of our stories in Top Stories. ## What NVLink Fusion does First unveiled in May 2025, NVLink Fusion is the interconnect technology that lets partners build semi-custom AI infrastructure. Non-Nvidia accelerators plug into Nvidia’s rack designs and networking, so a data centre can mix processor types without a separate rack architecture for each. d-Matrix [announced on 10 September](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/d-matrix-nvlink-fusion/) that it will use NVLink Fusion to connect its next-generation Raptor processors to Nvidia’s platform. Its racks are meant to work alongside Nvidia GPU systems such as Vera Rubin NVL72 for disaggregated inference, where different hardware handles different stages of a workload. “Demand for inference is soaring, but capital, time and energy remain finite,” said Sid Sheth, d-Matrix’s cofounder and CEO. [Reuters reported](https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/chip-startup-d-matrix-use-nvidia-chip-linking-tech-ai-servers-2026-09-10/) that Microsoft has backed the startup since a $110 million round in 2023. ## Why Nvidia would back a rival The logic is about staying central as customers diversify. Rivals’ chips that connect through Nvidia’s networking and racks still sit inside Nvidia’s infrastructure. Customers can add specialised hardware without abandoning their existing systems, and Nvidia keeps its role in the stack. It hedges against the inference market fragmenting into purpose-built chips, a shift Nvidia has also addressed with its Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator. d-Matrix is a sizeable bet. [Data Center Dynamics notes](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/report-nvidia-plans-to-invest-in-inference-chip-startup-d-matrix/) that it closed a $275 million Series C in November 2025 at a $2 billion valuation, and that The Information separately reported in July that it was seeking new financing at a $5 billion valuation. Reuters’ figures differ slightly, citing $450 million raised last year at the same $2 billion valuation. ## What it means for regional buyers Nothing in the reporting mentions the Gulf. Infra & Chips.content: ![share_log](https://pubimg.futunn.com/202205090000025243a644bb458.jpg?imageMogr2/thumbnail/76x76!/ignore-error/1/format/webp) ![](https://foss1.futunn.com/official_config_oss/prod/7be2ac47-b08d-41c9-9fd3-3ea14c7f1a22) * [Headlines](/en/main) * Global Research Selection | Bernstein Breaks Down AI Infrastructure Costs: Investment Peaks at $39.5 Billion per GW # Global Research Selection | Bernstein Breaks Down AI Infrastructure Costs: Investment Peaks at $39.5 Billion per GW [cls.cn](https://plb.futunn.com/link?target=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cls.cn%2Fdetail%2F2501306) ·  07:34 [AMD -2.03%](https://www.futunn.com/en/stock/AMD-US) [GOOG +0.87%](https://www.futunn.com/en/stock/GOOG-US) [GOOGL +0.97%](https://www.futunn.com/en/stock/GOOGL-US) [NVDA -0.52%](https://www.futunn.com/en/stock/NVDA-US) ① NVIDIA's Rubin cabinet cost is expected to decrease by 17% to $7.52 million, primarily due to adjustments in HBM and NAND estimates; ② AMD GPUs are priced lower, but memory and networking costs are higher, bringing the total cabinet price close to that of the Rubin; ③ Google's TPU single-system price is significantly lower than the Rubin, yet its construction costs are comparable at the same power-supply scale. Cailian Press, October 10 (Editor: Xia Junxiong) — A research report released by Bernstein on October 5 indicates that building a 1 GW data center using different AI accelerator architectures would require capital expenditures of approximately $34.6 billion to $39.5 billion. Among these, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture has the highest construction costs, while OpenAI's self-developed ASIC architecture, Jalapeno, is relatively lower. ![](https://image.cls.cn/images/20261010/e34V1nx8uO_1728x576.png) Although the price differences among various AI chips and server systems are substantial, once normalized to a common power‑supply capacity, the gap in overall data‑center construction costs narrows considerably. ![](https://record.futunn.com/news-editor-imgs/20261011/public/17916528150678900089997.png?imageMogr2/quality/minsize/1/ignore-error/1/format/webp)Bernstein has sharply lowered its estimate of NVIDIA's Rubin NVL72 single‑rack cost from the previous $9.1 million to $7.52 million, a reduction of about 17%, primarily reflecting adjustments to HBM pricing and NAND storage capacity expectations. The research report also points out that the primary financial burden of AI data centers is not electricity costs, but rather substantial capital expenditures and the resulting depreciation. As NVIDIA's Rubin and custom ASICs drive growth in computing power supply, the cost structure and return on investment of AI infrastructure are becoming central concerns for the industry. Investment in 1 GW of data centers could reach as high as US$40 billion. Bernstein conducted a cost comparison of the major AI accelerator architectures from NVIDIA, AMD, Google, and OpenAI, based on industry expert interviews, supply-chain surveys, corporate disclosures, and third-party data. The research team estimates that NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 single cabinet costs about $4.13 million, while the next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 reaches $7.52 million. AMD's MI455X Helios cabinet costs approximately $7.33 million, close to Rubin's price. ![](https://image.cls.cn/images/20261010/eyMHa2hZEF_1544x1112.png) (System Cost Composition Across Different AI Chip Architectures) By comparison, a single Google TPU v7 Ironwood system costs approximately $2.69 million, while OpenAI's Jalapeno system, which employs a two‑rack design, costs about $5.03 million. However, the price of a single system does not directly reflect the overall construction cost of a data center, as power consumption and hardware configurations vary significantly across different architectures. Advertisment [![banner](https://img-cdn.publive.online/fit-in/0x0/filters:format(webp)/indianstartupnews/media/media_files/2026/06/17/desktop-728-x-90-1-2026-06-17-17-20-35.png)](https://theindiandream.club/) The Nasdaq-listed company said the expansion will bring its AI cloud platform closer to Indian customers, providing enterprises with specialised computing infrastructure, software and services to develop, deploy and scale AI applications. The planned development will comprise three buildings, each with 80 MW of capacity, at AdaniConneX's Taloja campus in Navi Mumbai. CoreWeave will be the sole tenant across all three buildings, with an opportunity to add a further 240 MW at the site, potentially taking its total capacity there to 480 MW. The first phase is expected to become available in mid-2028, with additional capacity scheduled to come online in stages. The company has not disclosed the financial value of the proposed investment. ## CoreWeave to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform As part of the project, CoreWeave plans to deploy NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform on its AI cloud infrastructure in India to support workloads including AI model training, inference, reasoning and agentic AI applications. The Taloja facilities are being designed for high-density AI computing, with direct liquid cooling for graphics processing unit (GPU) data halls and a non-evaporative chilled water system. According to CoreWeave, the infrastructure is intended to accommodate future generations of AI computing technology as processing requirements evolve. The company also plans to establish an office in India and hire local employees to work with customers and partners. However, it has not specified the location of the proposed office, the number of employees it intends to recruit or a timeline for establishing its local operations. “India has the talent, developers, and ambition to become a major center of AI innovation,” said Sachin Jain, COO of CoreWeave. “We are investing in the infrastructure, technology, and local presence needed to support that growth, bringing 240 megawatts of capacity, NVIDIA Vera Rubin, and CoreWeave’s expertise to customers building and scaling AI in India,” he said. ## Expansion aligns with India's AI infras...

Infra & Chips.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) ![](https://img.youtube.com/vi/1Q_7yU7FZ1k/hqdefault.jpg) [The Memory Wall and the Future of AI Infrastructure | Pat Gelsinger on a16z](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1Q_7yU7FZ1k) HostRaghu RaghuramHostGuido Appenzeller 8 hours ago00:53:00en ## Key Takeaways Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger argues AI growth is now capped by flat US energy capacity and fab, packaging, and memory bottlenecks, so hardware builders should bet on optical IO, new memory, and power innovation. ## Summary Pat Gelsinger, who ran Intel and later VMware and is now a general partner at Playground Global, argues that AI has made chip design itself the easy part — and that the real constraints have moved to memory, manufacturing time, power, and cooling. Speaking with hosts Raghu Raghuram and Guido Appenzeller (both former VMware executives), Gelsinger says the industry is entering a hardware renaissance after 25 years in the wilderness, but that the bottleneck has shifted from design to everything downstream of it. The episode's title promises a case for building hardware now, and that case is present, but the conversation is mostly a technical tour of where AI infrastructure breaks: HBM's limits, the nine-month gap between finishing a design and using it, the flatlining of energy capacity in the US, and why 100 AI inference chip startups will not survive. Gelsinger also confirms he has personally funded a new stealth memory company, and predicts the first real memory innovation in 30 years is close. ## AI compressed design time, so the bottleneck moved to fabs, packaging, and racks Gelsinger's central structural claim is that AI tooling has collapsed the design phase while leaving every physical step untouched. If he and Appenzeller sat down to design a chip today, he says, AI tools could produce an excellent design in three months — but it would still take roughly nine months before that chip could actually be used at scale. That gap breaks the feedback loop: by the time silicon arrives, the AI workload assumptions that shaped the design are obsolete. He breaks the nine months into stages: three months minimum to get anything out of a fab even with supercharged design flows, another three months for advanced 3D packaging, and then rack-scale integration, because "nothing's a chip anymore, it's a rack." He points to GraphCore as a historical example of a design that was not bad but was overtaken by a world that moved on during the delay. > "It took me three months to design it, but it's nine months until I can actually start to use it." The fixes he names are new forms of lithography, design flows that do not require $50 million in mask costs before prototyping, and compression of the whole cycle to a month or two. He also flags power modeling as badly underdeveloped: today's tools lack good 3D modeling for power dissipation and hotspots, and he estimates roughly 40% of the power envelope is lost to guard banding. He draws a direct parallel to the 486, which he worked on as architect and design manager. That chip, he says, was the first to implement what became modern EDA — there was no Verilog, so Intel invented its own hardware description language, built a compiler for it, and worked with Alberto Sangiovanni-Vincentelli and his Berkeley students on the first automatic placement, routing, and timing management. His prediction is that people will look back at today's generation the way he looks back at the 486: as the beginning of a new era of AI-driven chip design. ## Memory is the hardest bottleneck, and Gelsinger has funded a stealth bet on it Gelsinger calls HBM "a hideous memory" and "just the best one that we've got" — terrible bit density, limited to shoreline bandwidth, with power and thermal problems, and DRAM does not like to be hot. The episode's title promises a case for building hardware now, and that case is present, but the conversation is mostly a technical tour of where AI infrastructure breaks: HBM's limits, the nine-month gap between finishing a design and using it, the flatlining of energy capacity in the US, and why 100 AI inference chip startups will not survive. Gelsinger also confirms he has personally funded a new stealth memory company, and predicts the first real memory innovation in 30 years is close. ## AI compressed design time, so the bottleneck moved to fabs, packaging, and racks Gelsinger's central structural claim is that AI tooling has collapsed the design phase while leaving every physical step untouched. If he and Appenzeller sat down to design a chip today, he says, AI tools could produce an excellent design in three months — but it would still take roughly nine months before that chip could actually be used at scale. That gap breaks the feedback loop: by the time silicon arrives, the AI workload assumptions that shaped the design are obsolete. He breaks the nine months into stages: three months minimum to get anything out of a fab even with supercharged design flows, another three months for advanced 3D packaging, and then rack-scale integration, because "nothing's a chip anymore, it's a rack." He points to GraphCore as a historical example of a design that was not bad but was overtaken by a world that moved on during the delay. > "It took me three months to design it, but it's nine months until I can actually start to use it." The fixes he names are new forms of lithography, design flows that do not require $50 million in mask costs before prototyping, and compression of the whole cycle to a month or two. He also flags power modeling as badly underdeveloped: today's tools lack good 3D modeling for power dissipation and hotspots, and he estimates roughly 40% of the power envelope is lost to guard banding. He draws a direct parallel to the 486, which he worked on as architect and design manager. That chip, he says, was the first to implement what became modern EDA — there was no Verilog, so Intel invented its own hardware description language, built a compiler for it, and worked with Alberto Sangiovanni-Vincentelli and his Berkeley students on the first automatic placement, routing, and timing management. His prediction is that people will look back at today's generation the way he looks back at the 486: as the beginning of a new era of AI-driven chip design. ## Memory is the hardest bottleneck, and Gelsinger has funded a stealth bet on it Gelsinger calls HBM "a hideous memory" and "just the best one that we've got" — terrible bit density, limited to shoreline bandwidth, with power and thermal problems, and DRAM does not like to be hot.
